Looking Back & Looking Forward
:::

## What I learned in this module

This module asked me to build something I had never built before - a fully functioning personal portfolio website using version-controlled code, deployed live on the internet. That might sound straightforward, but the process involved far more problem-solving, patience, and iteration than I expected.

---

## Git and Version Control

::: {.callout-note}
## Before this module
I had used Git before in order to download files/mods but have never used it in a structured way.
:::

Learning Git properly was one of the most practically useful things I took from this module. The core insight was: **every change is tracked, every mistake is recoverable**. 

I unfortunately have not utilised Git to full potential building a website without uploading every version to Git, which was a reason of a lot of headache as all the different version os documents were cluttering the desktop.

---

## Quarto and Web Publishing

I came into this module having built basic HTML pages but never having used a static site generator. Quarto's approach - write in Markdown, configure in YAML, and let the tool handle rendering - took some getting used to.

The main challenge was learning that Quarto has opinions about structure. Using the built-in navbar, listing pages, and About templates felt constraining at first, but I got used to these conventions, as they exist for good reasons: they produce accessible, consistent, and well-structured output with much less manual work.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Useful Quarto discovery
The `listing` feature for projects was far more powerful than I expected. Defining metadata in YAML frontmatter and letting Quarto generate a filterable, searchable grid automatically saved hours compared to maintaining a hand-coded HTML grid.
:::

---

## Design and Accessibility

I initially underestimated how much design decisions matter. A technically correct page that is hard to read or navigate reflects poorly on the work it contains.

Choosing a consistent colour palette (forest green and gold), setting up Sass variables so those colours were applied consistently, and making sure text had sufficient contrast all took longer than I expected - but the result felt more professional and more *mine* than a default template would have.

## Where I go from here

This module gave me a foundation I did not have before. I now understand how modern technical publishing works, how to manage code with version control, and how to deploy a live site from a local project. It reinforced that learning technical tools is mostly about tolerating confusion long enough and only then you get to build something real.

My next steps:

1. **Expand the projects section** as I complete more work in my MSc
2. **Add interactive visualisations** using Plotly as I develop stronger Python skills
3. **Contribute to open-source** projects on GitHub to build a public coding history
4. **Apply these skills professionally** in a graduate data analyst role
